newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: SBC Dillion buy would make sense - analysts.
newsitem.headline: SBC Dillion buy would make sense - analysts.

text.p: Swiss Bank Corp (SBC) declined comment on rumours of a purchase of U.S. investment bank Dillon Read & Co, but analysts said such a move would take SBC one step closer to rounding out operations and becoming a key global player.
The Wall Street Journal reported on Thursday that SBC Warburg, the investment banking unit of SBC, was expected to announce as early as Thursday a $600 million deal to buy the Dillon Read.

"If it happens it's a sensible move. Dillon has a good client list in the U.S. and doesn't have a lot of capital needs for big trading or book running operations," said James Hyde, Merrill Lynch banking analyst in London.

Speculation grew after news on Wednesday that the Dutch financial services group ING Groep NV, which owns 25 percent of Dillion Read, had broken off talks to buy the remaining 75 percent from the firm's partners.
Both SBC and its Swiss rival UBS have made no secret of the fact that they are interested in expanding, preferably through acquisition, in the vast U.S. market.
UBS wants to be bigger in asset management and private banking, and SBC in investment banking.
Largely as the result of its acquisition of S.G. Warburg in mid-1995, SBC's operations just about fit the bill in most regions outside the United States.
"If you strip out the U.S. they are in a very good position...they are number two in the Euromarkets," Hyde said.
However, SBC has said it would remain cautious with regard to North America, holding back while assessing the changes in the U.S. regulatory environment.
But expansion in the United States is important for any financial institution seeking a place at the table with the truly global banking players in the next century.
SBC chief executive Marcel Ospel said last month that the company had no plans for a major investment banking acquisition in North America.
He also dismissed the idea of buying a second-tier U.S. investment bank, but said the bank would consider acquiring a franchise or expertise through the purchase of a small boutique.
Waiting too long to expand in the United States could put SBC, and for that matter any other outside bank, at a disadvantage if they allow the U.S. banks to get a head start on their home ground.
"The big U.S. banks are overcapitalised and will have a lot of muscle to move in too," Bank Vontobel analyst Susanne Borer said.
The union of investment banks and commercial banks in the United States has long been anticipated amid the gradual erosion of the 1933 Glass-Steagall law.

The law is still in effect, but the Federal Reserve raised the limit this year on how much underwriting a bank can do through its securities affiliate to 25 percent from a prior 10 percent. U.S. banks have already begun to take advantage of the changes.

Dillon Read is not a major player and thus would not immediately push SBC to the top of the heap in the U.S. investment banking community. But Dillon has a good reputation, a good client book and capable management, analysts said.
"The key relationships (with Dillion management and their corporate finance contacts) will make or break the deal," Salomon Brothers banking analyst John Leonard said.
"A price of $600 million is three times book value. It looks expensive, but could be financed quite easily (by SBC)," Pictet & Cie equities analyst Claudia von Tuerk said.
